headline: Study: most online creators earn less than you think

sources.title: A 67% Majority of Creators Earn Less Than $10,000 per Year, Study Finds (TheWrap)
CreatorIQ Study Reveals a Growing Authenticity Gap (CreatorIQ)
67% Of Creators Earn Under $10,000 A Year While Pay Still Favors Reach, Study Finds (NetInfluencer)

chunks.text: Being an online [[creator]] looks like a [[dream job]]. But a large new study says the money is much smaller than most fans imagine. Researchers [[surveyed]] 5,095 creators in around 100 [[regions]] this year. Two thirds said their videos and posts {{bring in}} less than ten thousand dollars a year. Six in ten creators cannot {{get by}} on what they earn online, so many {{turn to}} teaching, office work, or delivery jobs to pay the [[bills]].

verbs.correct: To earn money for a person or business
verbs.wrong: To count coins at the end of a day
verbs.why: A job brings in a steady paycheck, and a small business can bring in extra profit in a good month. In this study, two out of three creators said their videos and posts bring in less than ten thousand dollars a year.

verbs.correct: To survive with just enough money
verbs.wrong: To save money for the future
verbs.why: Families get by on one salary, students get by on cheap food, and workers get by on a small paycheck. In this study, six out of ten creators say they cannot get by on what they earn from their online work.

verbs.correct: To use something as a source of help
verbs.why: People turn to friends for advice, turn to a lawyer for help, or turn to prayer in hard times. Many creators in this study turn to teaching, office jobs, or delivery work to pay their bills.

chunks.text: The study also shows how hard the work is. Creators often spend years {{building up}} a [[following]] from zero. They must {{keep up with}} new [[trends]], new apps, and [[constant]] posting [[schedules]]. And with millions of [[channels]] online, it is hard to {{stand out}} in a crowded [[feed]]. The report found that pay follows size: creators with more [[followers]] and views earn more, even when smaller channels get warmer comments from their fans.

verbs.correct: To grow something slowly over time
verbs.wrong: To repair something old and broken
verbs.why: Runners build up strength week by week, savers build up a bank account, and companies build up a reputation over time. Creators in this study often spend years building up a following that started at zero.

verbs.wrong: To watch something from far away
verbs.why: Workers keep up with new technology, students keep up with homework, and fans keep up with the latest news. Creators in this study must keep up with new trends, new apps, and constant posting schedules.

verbs.correct: To be easy to notice among others
verbs.wrong: To wait quietly in a long line
verbs.why: A bright red coat can stand out in a crowd, and one strong answer can stand out on a job application. With millions of channels online, the study says it is hard for any single creator to stand out.

chunks.text: So who actually makes money? Only a small group at the top. Almost every big name {{started out}} small, with few fans and years of low pay. The winners often {{cash in on}} their [[fame]] by selling their own products: about half of the creators in the study have [[launched]] their own [[brand]] or plan to start one. Most [[top earners]] still depend on paid posts for companies, mostly on Instagram and TikTok. But many others {{give up}} and go back to [[full-time]] jobs when the money stays small.

verbs.correct: To begin a career or journey
verbs.why: Many chefs start out washing dishes, and many companies start out in a garage with little money. The study found that almost every famous creator started out small, with only a few fans and years of low pay.

verbs.correct: To make money from a success
verbs.wrong: To lose money on a bad plan
verbs.why: Stores cash in on holiday shopping, and singers sometimes cash in on a hit song with a world tour. The most successful creators in this study cash in on their fame by launching their own brand of products.

verbs.correct: To stop trying to do something
verbs.why: People give up on a diet after one bad week, and some students give up on a hard class too soon. Many creators in this study give up and return to full-time jobs once the money stays small.

chunks.text: The report's advice is honest: treat creating like a slow business, not a [[lottery ticket]]. Most successful creators earn from many places, like [[ads]], [[tips]], and product sales, and the small numbers {{add up}} month after month. For a [[patient]] few, the years of work finally {{pay off}} with a real [[career]]. The study found one more surprise: 42 percent of creators worry that deals with companies could cost them their fans' [[trust]]. Even in a dream job, nothing is free.

verbs.correct: To slowly become a large amount
verbs.why: Small daily coffee purchases add up fast, and minutes of daily practice add up to real skill over a year. In this study, small payments from ads, tips, and sales add up month after month for patient creators.

verbs.correct: To bring success after hard work
verbs.wrong: To cause problems after a delay
verbs.why: Years of studying can pay off on exam day, and early morning practice can pay off at the big game. The study says that for a patient few, years of effort finally pay off with a real, lasting career.

mainIdea.s: A big new study of more than five thousand creators found that most earn under ten thousand dollars a year. Many need other jobs, and only a small group gets rich.
mainIdea.why: 67 percent of the 5,095 creators surveyed bring in less than that, and six in ten cannot get by on online money alone.

mainIdea.s: A new study found that most online creators earn around ten thousand a month from their videos. Half of them also make extra money selling their own brands.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the study says under ten thousand a YEAR, not a month. The brand number is real, but the pay number is flipped.

mainIdea.s: The biggest video apps promised to pay every small creator a salary starting next year. The plan is meant to help tiny channels compete with famous stars.
mainIdea.why: The article reports a survey about what creators already earn. No app promised anyone a salary.

tf.s: Two thirds of the creators said their content brings in less than ten thousand dollars a year
tf.why: The survey of 5,095 creators found 67 percent earn under that amount from their posts and videos.

tf.s: Most creators can easily get by on their online money alone
tf.why: Six in ten cannot get by on it, so many turn to teaching, office work, or delivery jobs.

tf.s: The study says warm comments matter more for pay than follower numbers
tf.why: Pay follows size. Creators with more followers and views earn more, even when small channels get warmer comments.

tf.s: About half of the creators have launched their own brand or plan to start one
tf.why: Top creators often cash in on their fame by selling their own products.

tf.s: The report compares creating to a lottery ticket that pays off fast
tf.why: It says the opposite. Creating is a slow business where small numbers add up month after month.

tf.s: Some creators worry that deals with companies could cost them their fans' trust
tf.why: 42 percent worry that such deals could damage the trust they built up with their audience.
